item.title: Temperature Sampling: Why Your Stock Agent Keeps Changing Its Mind
item.author: lunke.qing@gmail.com (Lunke)
item.description:
Your stock-analysis agent might give you a clear verdict yesterday. Today, same data, same question — and it says the opposite. Not a little different. Contradictory.

Before you blame the model, the prompt, or the data pipeline: check the one number almost nobody talks about.

某LLM：Oooops，上次是我搞错了，主力正在加速撤逃。。。（纯玩梗，无恶意）

Temperature
#

It’s a single parameter, usually one line in a JSON payload, and it quietly decides whether your agent behaves like a forensic accountant or a drunken idea guy. Most people set it once, never touch it again, and then wonder why their “AI system” is unreliable.

Here’s the thing: temperature isn’t a magic quality dial. It’s a sampling parameter, and once you see the two lines of math behind it, you’ll know exactly why your analysis agent flip-flops — and how to make it stop. By the end of this post, you’ll be able to tune your own stock agent for stable, reproducible analysis, and you’ll finally understand what people mean when they say “low temperature for facts, high temperature for creativity.”

item.title: System, User, Assistant: The Three Roles Behind Every LLM Conversation
item.author: lunke.qing@gmail.com (Lunke)
item.description:
You type a question into a chat window, hit Enter, and a reply streams back. The UI is smooth, the cursor blinks, and somewhere a GPU wakes up. But what actually happened between your keystroke and that first token? Most people who “use” LLMs daily have never seen the actual shape of the request their chat client fires off. It’s not a box of text. It’s a list.

A message array. And inside that list, every entry wears one of three hats: system, user, or assistant. This article is about what those hats mean, why they exist, and why — once you understand them — you’ll never look at an LLM call the same way again.

item.title: Context Window: The Model's Whiteboard (and Why 1M Isn't a Free Pass)
item.author: lunke.qing@gmail.com (Lunke)
item.description:
Every model launch now brags about context length. “1M context window!” sounds like the model can swallow an entire book series in one gulp.

But 1M is not a free pass. Here’s the reality check: if you stuff 900K tokens of input into a 1M window, you only have ~100K left for the output. And even if you somehow fill all of it, the model won’t “remember” everything equally well.

So what is a context window, really? And why does it behave in all these counterintuitive ways?

item.title: BPE(Byte Pair Encoding)：大模型是怎么"看"文字的
item.author: lunke.qing@gmail.com (Lunke)
item.description:
接触大模型的人都绕不开一个词：Token。计费按 token、上下文窗口按 token、性能优化还是围绕 token，它是模型世界的"货币"。

但 Token 到底是什么？为什么教科书说它"不是字也不是词"？背后的 BPE 分词算法又是怎么工作的？

这篇文章不堆公式，用乐高工厂的比喻，带你手把手跑一遍 BPE 的全过程。走完你就懂了。
